claims.claim: > **Quick answer:** Compounded tirzepatide and Zepbound are not the same regulatory product. FDA identifies Zepbound as a tirzepatide injection and lists it as prescription. FDA says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and are not reviewed before marketing for safety, effectiveness, or quality. A shared ingredient does not prove equivalence. [S1][S2][S4][S6]

The current FDA-hosted label identifies Zepbound as a tirzepatide injection for subcutaneous use. [S4] The Drugs@FDA application record lists ZEPBOUND, active ingredient TIRZEPATIDE, a solution for subcutaneous administration, and prescription marketing status. [S6]

FDA’s compounding Q&A states that compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. [S2] FDA’s unapproved-GLP-1 statement says the agency does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed. [S1]
| Ingredient identity | Whether a source names tirzepatide as an ingredient; it does not establish a finished product or a batch. [S4] |
| Approved product | The Zepbound brand, FDA application, label, dosage form, and labeled indications. [S4][S6] |
| Compounded preparation | A named prescription-specific preparation, compounder, setting, formulation, presentation, and dated batch records, if supplied. [S2] |

The FDA label names ZEPBOUND as tirzepatide injection for subcutaneous use. [S4] Lilly’s prescribing information uses the same product identity and describes Zepbound as an injection. [S5] These sources are product-specific: they describe the labeled product supplied under the Zepbound name, not every preparation that uses the active-ingredient name tirzepatide.

The label excerpt identifies Zepbound as a GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist and states that it is indicated with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for labeled adult populations. It also includes an indication for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. [S4][S5] Those are label statements, not a conclusion that any reader meets an indication or should use a particular medicine.

The label also lists presentations in strengths of 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 7.5 mg, 10 mg, 12.5 mg, and 15 mg per 0.5 mL in a single-dose pen or single-dose vial. [S4] A presentation list is an identity and labeling fact. It is not a personal dose plan, a recommendation to change products, or a comparison of an unapproved preparation.

The Drugs@FDA record gives a second layer of identity evidence. It lists the active ingredient, dosage form and route, prescription marketing status. It also shows an ORIG-1 approval action dated November 8, 2023. [S6] An application record and a label answer different questions: the application record helps establish the regulatory record, while the label supplies the product-specific prescribing information.
| Brand and ingredient | ZEPBOUND; tirzepatide. [S4][S6] |
| Route and form | Injection; subcutaneous use. [S4][S6] |
| Marketing status | Prescription in the Drugs@FDA record. [S6] |
| Approval record | ORIG-1 action type listed as Approval on November 8, 2023. [S6] |
| Presentation excerpt | 2.5 mg through 15 mg per 0.5 mL in listed pen or vial presentations. [S4] |

FDA’s compounding Q&A explains that compounding can serve an important patient need when a patient cannot be treated with an FDA-approved medication, such as needing a different dosage form or avoiding an ingredient that causes an allergy. [S2] That explanation describes a possible role for compounding; it does not decide whether a particular preparation is necessary or appropriate for a particular person.

FDA also says compounded drugs should only be used in patients whose medical needs cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug. [S2] This is a source-bound regulatory statement. It is not permission to assume that a named website, pharmacy, or prescription has satisfied every applicable requirement.

The FDA Q&A distinguishes outsourcing facilities under section 503B from pharmacies and physicians operating under section 503A conditions. Drugs compounded in outsourcing facilities are subject to current good manufacturing practice requirements, while the cited section 503A category is not subject to those same CGMP requirements. [S2] This distinction is not a universal quality ranking. It means the legal and oversight setting matters and must be identified before a claim is evaluated.
| Legal setting | Named compounder and whether the source identifies a 503A or 503B setting; a general label is not enough. [S2] |
| Clinical context | A prescription-specific medical-need determination; this guide does not make one. [S2] |

FDA’s current unapproved-GLP-1 statement says compounded drugs are not FDA approved and that the agency does not review them for safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed. [S1] Among the warning signs FDA lists is a company claiming that a compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug. [S1]
| “Zepbound contains tirzepatide.” | Supported by the FDA label and Drugs@FDA record. [S4][S6] |
| “Compounded drugs are FDA-approved versions of Zepbound.” | Not supported; FDA states compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. [S1][S2] |
| “The products share an ingredient name.” | Can be stated only for the specific records that name the ingredient; it does not prove finished-product equivalence. [S4] |
The FDA policy page includes a dated April 1, 2026 update reminding compounders that certain conditions must be met for compounded drugs to qualify for the 503A and 503B exemptions. [S3]

The same FDA page states that tirzepatide and semaglutide do not currently appear on the 503B bulks list or FDA’s drug shortage list. [S3] This statement should not be rewritten as a permanent statement about every compounding pathway, every state rule, every pharmacy, or every future date.

FDA's press announcement reports that FDA proposed excluding tirzepatide, semaglutide, and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list after finding no clinical need for outsourcing facilities to compound those substances from bulk drug substances. [S8] The source describes a proposal. A proposal is not the same as a final transaction-level finding.

| What do the captured FDA excerpts say? | FDA reminded compounders on April 1, 2026 that 503A and 503B exemptions have conditions. The same FDA page separately states that tirzepatide and semaglutide do not currently appear on the 503B bulks list or FDA's shortage list. [S3] |

| What did the captured FDA 503B bulks-list proposal say? | FDA said it was proposing to exclude tirzepatide from the 503B bulks list after finding no clinical need for outsourcing facilities to compound it from bulk drug substance. [S8] |
| Does a proposal prove a final legal conclusion for every pathway? | No. The source describes a proposal, not an individualized or transaction-level conclusion. [S8] |

2. **Locate the authority.** Use the FDA label or Drugs@FDA record for Zepbound identity and approval-record facts. Use FDA compounding sources for general pathway statements. Do not use a provider landing page as a substitute for a regulator’s product record. [S1][S2][S4][S6]
3. **Check the date.** A shortage or 503B statement can be time-bound. Preserve the date instead of presenting an old policy snapshot as a current guarantee. [S3][S8]
5. **Separate label from outcome.** Zepbound’s labeled indications and presentations do not predict an individual’s safety, effectiveness, eligibility, response, or outcome. [S4]

7. **Reject the equivalence shortcut.** Shared ingredient wording does not prove identical formulation, presentation, manufacturing controls, labeling, clinical evidence, or batch quality. Among the warning signs FDA lists is a company claiming that a compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug. [S1]
| Zepbound is identified in the current FDA label as tirzepatide injection for subcutaneous use. [S4] | That an unnamed compounded preparation is equivalent to Zepbound. |
| Drugs@FDA lists Zepbound as tirzepatide, subcutaneous solution, and prescription. [S6] | A reader’s eligibility, prescription need, dose, or switching plan. |

| FDA says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and are not reviewed by FDA before marketing for safety, effectiveness, or quality. [S1][S2] | A specific compounder’s compliance, a batch’s quality, or an individual’s safety or outcome. |
| FDA dated a 503B conditions statement April 1, 2026 and separately published proposal language. [S3][S8] | A current price, coverage result, inventory status, shipping promise, or savings amount. |

No same-product conclusion is established here. Zepbound is an FDA-identified tirzepatide injection with a product label and application record. Among the warning signs FDA lists is a company claiming that a compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug. Shared ingredient wording alone does not prove identical formulation, presentation, controls, labeling, or batch quality. [S1][S4][S6]

FDA’s compounding Q&A states that compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. That is a category-level statement, not a finding about one unnamed preparation. A specific preparation also requires its own identity, prescription, compounder, setting, and current records before additional claims can be evaluated. [S2]

No transfer is established. The FDA label identifies Zepbound as a specific tirzepatide injection and provides Zepbound-specific indications and presentations. Those statements remain attached to that product record. They do not supply a label, approval, or outcome conclusion for a different compounded preparation. [S4]

No. The captured FDA conditions statement is dated. A separate captured sentence describes list status, and the FDA 503B proposal capture describes a proposal. Neither source is a current named-facility, prescription, batch, or transaction determination. Read the current primary source and obtain the records relevant to the exact claim. [S3][S8]

First identify whether the page means ingredient identity or finished-product equivalence. Then check the exact approved product, compounded preparation, pathway, presentation, date, and transaction. Among the warning signs FDA lists is a company claiming that a compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug. If the page does not supply the evidence for a field, record it as `Not stated`. [S1]

FDA’s label identifies Zepbound as a tirzepatide injection, and Drugs@FDA lists TIRZEPATIDE as the active ingredient. [S4][S6] That product identity does not make every preparation using tirzepatide Zepbound.

For the question compounded tirzepatide vs Zepbound, start with the regulatory distinction. Zepbound has a product-specific FDA label and application record identifying tirzepatide injection. FDA says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and are not reviewed before marketing for safety, effectiveness, or quality. [S1][S2][S4][S6]

The FDA label states that the most common adverse reactions reported in at least 5% of patients treated with Zepbound are nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, injection site reactions, fatigue, hypersensitivity reactions, eructation, hair loss, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). [S4]

For weight reduction, Studies 1 and 2 were randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled fixed-dosage trials in adults. Studies 5 and 6 included 467 adults with moderate to severe OSA and obesity. [S4]
These Zepbound records do not establish comparable safety, effectiveness, or outcomes for a compounded preparation; FDA says compounded drugs lack premarket safety or effectiveness review. [S1][S4]

FDA’s Zepbound label has a boxed warning: tirzepatide caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rats; whether Zepbound causes these tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans is unknown. Zepbound is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of MTC, or in patients with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). [S4]

FDA reports dosing errors with compounded injectable semaglutide, including some reports requiring hospitalization. Separately, FDA reports adverse events that may be related to compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide prescribed beyond FDA-approved label doses. These are distinct reports, not established tirzepatide-specific dosing-error or hospitalization rates. [S1]

FDA warns that illegally marketed semaglutide and tirzepatide may be counterfeit, contain wrong or harmful ingredients, or contain too little, too much, or no active ingredient. This warning concerns illegally marketed products; it does not identify every compounded drug as counterfeit. [S1]
